questions.q: A coil offers a resistance of $20 \mathrm{~ohm}$ for a direct current. If we send an alternating current through the same coil, the resistance offered by the coil to the alternating current will be :
questions.solution:
A coil is characterized by its resistance $R$ and its self-inductance $L$. When a direct current (DC) flows through the coil, the frequency $f$ is $0$, so the inductive reactance $X_L = 2\pi f L = 0$. Thus, the total impedance $Z$ for DC is equal to the resistance $R = 20 \Omega$.

When an alternating current (AC) flows through the coil, the frequency $f \gt 0$, which results in an inductive reactance $X_L = 2\pi f L \gt 0$. The impedance $Z$ for AC is given by $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$.

Since $X_L \gt 0$, it follows that $Z = \sqrt{20^2 + X_L^2} \gt \sqrt{20^2} = 20 \Omega$. Therefore, the coil offers a greater resistance (impedance) to the alternating current compared to the direct current.

Answer: Greater than $20 \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A transformer which steps down $330 \mathrm{~V}$ to $33 \mathrm{~V}$ is to operate a device having impedance $110 \Omega$. The current drawn by the primary coil of the transformer is :
questions.solution:
The secondary voltage $V_s$ is $33 \text{ V}$ and the impedance of the device connected to the secondary coil is $Z = 110 \Omega$.

The current in the secondary coil $I_s$ is given by Ohm's law:

$I_s = \dfrac{V_s}{Z} = \dfrac{33}{110} = 0.3 \text{ A}$

For an ideal transformer, the power input equals the power output, so $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$.

Given the primary voltage $V_p = 330 \text{ V}$, we have:

$330 \times I_p = 33 \times 0.3$

$I_p = \dfrac{33 \times 0.3}{330} = \dfrac{0.3}{10} = 0.03 \text{ A}$

Answer: 0.03 A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The difference in energy levels of an electron at two excited levels is $13.75 \mathrm{~eV}$. If it makes a transition from the higher energy level to the lower energy level then what will be the wave length of the emitted radiation?
[given $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~m}^2 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} ; c=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1} ; 1 \mathrm{~eV}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}$]
questions.solution:
The energy difference between the two levels is given by $\Delta E = 13.75 \text{ eV}$.

Converting this energy into Joules:
$\Delta E = 13.75 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 22 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$.

The relationship between energy and wavelength is $\Delta E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

Rearranging for wavelength $\lambda$:
$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$.

Substituting the given values $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$:
$\lambda = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{22 \times 10^{-19}}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{19.8 \times 10^{-26}}{22 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.9 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.

Converting to Angstroms ($\text{A}$):
$\lambda = 0.9 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{10} \text{ A} = 0.9 \times 10^3 \text{ A} = 900 \text{ A}$.

Answer: $900^{\circ} \mathrm{A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is $400 \mathrm{~pF}$. It is connected to an ac source of $100 \mathrm{~V}$ having an angular frequency $100 \mathrm{~rad~s}^{-1}$. If the rms value of the current is $4 \mu \mathrm{A}$, the displacement current is:
questions.solution:
The displacement current $I_d$ in a parallel plate capacitor is defined as the current flowing through the circuit, which is equal to the conduction current $I_c$ in the connecting wires.

The relationship between the conduction current and the displacement current is given by $I_d = I_c$.

Given that the rms value of the current in the circuit is $I_{rms} = 4 \mu \text{A}$, this current represents the conduction current flowing through the wires connected to the capacitor plates.

According to the principle of continuity of current, the displacement current between the plates of the capacitor must be equal to the conduction current in the external circuit.

Therefore, $I_d = I_{rms} = 4 \mu \text{A}$.

Answer: 4 $\mu$A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor is filled by a dielectric whose relative permittivity varies with the applied voltage (U) as $\epsilon=2 U$. A similar capacitor with no dielectric is charged to $U_0=78 \mathrm{~V}$. It is then connected to the uncharged capacitor with the dielectric. Find the final voltage on the capacitors.
questions.solution:
Let $C_0$ be the capacitance of the capacitor without the dielectric. The charge on this capacitor is $Q_0 = C_0 U_0$, where $U_0 = 78$ V.

When the two capacitors are connected in parallel, the total charge $Q_0$ is shared between them. Let $U$ be the final common voltage. The charge on the first capacitor is $Q_1 = C_0 U$.

The second capacitor has a dielectric with relative permittivity $\epsilon = 2U$. The capacitance of this capacitor is $C = \epsilon C_0 = (2U) C_0$. The charge on this capacitor is $Q_2 = C U = (2U) C_0 U = 2 C_0 U^2$.

By the principle of conservation of charge, $Q_0 = Q_1 + Q_2$.

$C_0 U_0 = C_0 U + 2 C_0 U^2$.

Dividing by $C_0$, we get $U_0 = U + 2U^2$.

Substituting $U_0 = 78$, we have $2U^2 + U - 78 = 0$.

Solving the quadratic equation for $U$ using the quadratic formula $U = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$:

$U = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1^2 - 4(2)(-78)}}{2(2)} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 624}}{4} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{625}}{4} = \dfrac{-1 \pm 25}{4}$.

Since voltage must be positive, $U = \dfrac{24}{4} = 6$ V.

Answer: 6V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Which of the following statement is true regarding the centre of mass of a system?
options: The centre of mass of a body always lies inside the body.
The centre of mass depends on the size and shape but does not depend on the distribution of mass of the body.
The centre of mass depends on the coordinate system.
The centre of mass of a system depends on the size and shape of the body but independent of the co-ordinate system
questions.solution:
The centre of mass of a system is defined by the position vector $\vec{R}_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}$.

The centre of mass is a point that represents the average position of the mass in a system. It depends on the distribution of mass, the size, and the shape of the body. However, the location of the centre of mass is a physical property of the body itself and is independent of the choice of the coordinate system used to describe it.

Option (1) is incorrect because the centre of mass can lie outside the body (e.g., a ring or a hollow sphere).

Option (2) is incorrect because the centre of mass is highly dependent on the distribution of mass.

Option (3) is incorrect because the physical location of the centre of mass is invariant under a change of coordinate system.

Option (4) correctly states that the centre of mass depends on the size, shape, and mass distribution of the body, while being independent of the coordinate system chosen.

Answer: The centre of mass of a system depends on the size and shape of the body but independent of the co-ordinate system

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Which of the following graph shows the variation of velocity with mass for the constant momentum?
questions.solution:
The relationship between momentum $p$, mass $m$, and velocity $v$ is given by the formula $p = mv$.

For a constant momentum $p$, the equation becomes $v = \dfrac{p}{m}$.

This equation represents an inverse proportionality between velocity $v$ and mass $m$, which is of the form $v \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$.

The graph of $v$ versus $m$ for an inverse relationship $v = \dfrac{k}{m}$ (where $k$ is a positive constant) is a rectangular hyperbola in the first quadrant, which corresponds to Fig 1.

Answer: Fig 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resistance of the galvanometer and shunt of an ammeter are $90 \mathrm{~ohm}$ and $10 \mathrm{~ohm}$ respectively, then the fraction of the main current passing through the galvanometer and the shut respectively are:
questions.solution:
Let $I$ be the total current, $I_g$ be the current through the galvanometer, and $I_s$ be the current through the shunt.

Given the resistance of the galvanometer $G = 90 \, \Omega$ and the resistance of the shunt $S = 10 \, \Omega$.

Since the galvanometer and shunt are connected in parallel, the potential difference across them is the same:

$I_g G = I_s S$

$I_g (90) = I_s (10)$

$I_s = 9 I_g$

The total current $I$ is given by $I = I_g + I_s$. Substituting $I_s = 9 I_g$ into this equation:

$I = I_g + 9 I_g = 10 I_g$

The fraction of the main current passing through the galvanometer is $\dfrac{I_g}{I} = \dfrac{I_g}{10 I_g} = \dfrac{1}{10}$.

The fraction of the main current passing through the shunt is $\dfrac{I_s}{I} = \dfrac{9 I_g}{10 I_g} = \dfrac{9}{10}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{10}$ and $\dfrac{9}{10}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $500 \mathrm{~W}$ heating unit is designed to operate on a $400 \mathrm{~V}$ line. If line voltage drops to $160 \mathrm{~V}$, the percentage drop in heat output will be:
questions.solution:
The power $P$ consumed by a heating unit is given by the formula $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$, where $V$ is the voltage and $R$ is the resistance of the heating element.

Since the resistance $R$ is constant, the power is proportional to the square of the voltage, $P \propto V^2$.

Let $P_1 = 500 \text{ W}$ at $V_1 = 400 \text{ V}$. When the voltage drops to $V_2 = 160 \text{ V}$, the new power $P_2$ is given by:

$\dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = \left( \dfrac{V_2}{V_1} \right)^2$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{P_2}{500} = \left( \dfrac{160}{400} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{2}{5} \right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{25}$

$P_2 = 500 \times \dfrac{4}{25} = 20 \times 4 = 80 \text{ W}$

The drop in heat output is $P_1 - P_2 = 500 - 80 = 420 \text{ W}$.

The percentage drop in heat output is $\dfrac{P_1 - P_2}{P_1} \times 100 = \dfrac{420}{500} \times 100 = \dfrac{420}{5} = 84\%$.

Answer: 84%

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The current through a conductor is '$\mathrm{a}$' when the temperature is $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. It is '$\mathrm{b}$' when the temperature is $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The current through the conductor at $220^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is
questions.solution:
The resistance of a conductor at temperature $T$ is given by $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha T)$, where $R_0$ is the resistance at $0^{\circ} \text{C}$ and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of resistance.

Given the current $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$, where $V$ is the constant applied voltage, we have $I_T = \dfrac{V}{R_0(1 + \alpha T)} = \dfrac{I_0}{1 + \alpha T}$.

At $T = 0^{\circ} \text{C}$, $I_0 = a$. Thus, $I_T = \dfrac{a}{1 + \alpha T}$.

At $T = 100^{\circ} \text{C}$, $I = b$. Substituting this into the equation: $b = \dfrac{a}{1 + 100\alpha} \Rightarrow 1 + 100\alpha = \dfrac{a}{b} \Rightarrow 100\alpha = \dfrac{a}{b} - 1 = \dfrac{a - b}{b} \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{a - b}{100b}$.

We need the current at $T = 220^{\circ} \text{C}$. Let this be $I_{220}$.

$I_{220} = \dfrac{a}{1 + 220\alpha} = \dfrac{a}{1 + 220 \times \left( \dfrac{a - b}{100b} \right)} = \dfrac{a}{1 + \dfrac{22}{10} \times \dfrac{a - b}{b}} = \dfrac{a}{1 + \dfrac{11(a - b)}{5b}}$.

$I_{220} = \dfrac{a}{\dfrac{5b + 11a - 11b}{5b}} = \dfrac{5ab}{11a - 6b}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{5 a b}{11 a-6 b}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: On increasing the temperature of a conductor, its resistance increases because
options: Number of collisions between electrons decreases
questions.solution:
The resistance of a conductor is given by the formula $R = \dfrac{ml}{ne^{2}A\tau}$, where $m$ is the mass of the electron, $l$ is the length of the conductor, $n$ is the number density of free electrons, $e$ is the charge of the electron, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $\tau$ is the relaxation time.

When the temperature of a conductor increases, the thermal velocity of the free electrons increases. This leads to more frequent collisions between the electrons and the lattice ions.

As a result of these more frequent collisions, the average time interval between two successive collisions, known as the relaxation time $\tau$, decreases.

Since $R$ is inversely proportional to $\tau$, a decrease in $\tau$ causes the resistance $R$ to increase.

Answer: Relaxation time decreases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A cell of emf E and internal resistance r is connected to two external resistances $\mathrm{R_1}$ and $\mathrm{R_2}$ and a perfect ammeter. The current in the circuit is measured in four different situations:
(a) without any external resistance in the circuit.
(b) with resistance $\mathrm{R_1}$ only
(c) with $\mathrm{R_1}$ and $\mathrm{R_2}$ in series combination.
(d) with $\mathrm{R_1}$ and $\mathrm{R_2}$ in parallel combination.
The currents measured in the four cases in ascending order are
questions.solution:
The current $I$ in a circuit with a cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ connected to an external resistance $R_{ext}$ is given by $I = \dfrac{E}{r + R_{ext}}$.

The four cases for $R_{ext}$ are:
(a) $R_{ext} = 0$, so $I_a = \dfrac{E}{r}$.
(b) $R_{ext} = R_1$, so $I_b = \dfrac{E}{r + R_1}$.
(c) $R_{ext} = R_1 + R_2$, so $I_c = \dfrac{E}{r + R_1 + R_2}$.
(d) $R_{ext} = \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$, so $I_d = \dfrac{E}{r + \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}}$.

Comparing the denominators:
Since $R_1 + R_2 \gt R_1 \gt \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \gt 0$, the denominators follow the order $r + R_1 + R_2 \gt r + R_1 \gt r + \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \gt r$.

Since the current is inversely proportional to the denominator, the currents follow the reverse order:
$\dfrac{E}{r + R_1 + R_2} \lt \dfrac{E}{r + R_1} \lt \dfrac{E}{r + \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}} \lt \dfrac{E}{r}$.

Therefore, $I_c \lt I_b \lt I_d \lt I_a$.

Answer: c < b < d < a

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The mass of a particle $\mathrm{A}$ is double that of the particle $\mathrm{B}$ and the kinetic energy of $\mathrm{B}$ is $\dfrac{1}{8}$th that of A then the ratio of the de- Broglie wavelength of A to that of B is:
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$

Given: $m_A = 2m_B$ and $K_B = \dfrac{1}{8}K_A \Rightarrow K_A = 8K_B$

$\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_B K_B}{m_A K_A}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_B \cdot K_B}{2m_B \cdot 8K_B}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$\lambda_A : \lambda_B = 1 : 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The threshold frequency for a metal surface is '$n_0$'. A photo electric current '$I$' is produced when it is exposed to a light of frequency $\left(\dfrac{11}{6}\right) \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}$ and intensity $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{n}}$. If both the frequency and intensity are halved, the new photoelectric current '$\mathrm{I}^1$' will become:
questions.solution:
The photoelectric effect occurs only when the incident frequency $ u$ is greater than or equal to the threshold frequency $ u_0$.

Initially, the incident frequency is $ u_1 = \dfrac{11}{6} u_0$. Since $ u_1 \gt u_0$, photoelectric emission occurs, and the current is $I$.

When the frequency is halved, the new frequency becomes $ u_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} imes \dfrac{11}{6} u_0 = \dfrac{11}{12} u_0$.

Comparing $ u_2$ with the threshold frequency $ u_0$, we observe that $ u_2 = \dfrac{11}{12} u_0 \lt u_0$.

Since the new incident frequency is less than the threshold frequency, no photoelectric emission can take place, regardless of the intensity of the light.

Therefore, the new photoelectric current $I^1$ is $0$.

Answer: $\mathrm{I^1=0}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Select the unit of the coefficient of mutual induction from the following.
questions.solution:
The coefficient of mutual induction $M$ is defined by the relation $\phi = M I$, where $\phi$ is the magnetic flux and $I$ is the current.

From this relation, $M = \dfrac{\phi}{I}$. The unit of magnetic flux $\phi$ is Weber (Wb) and the unit of current $I$ is Ampere (A). Thus, the unit of $M$ is Weber/Ampere.

Alternatively, using Faraday's law of induction, the induced electromotive force $\varepsilon$ is given by $\varepsilon = -M \dfrac{dI}{dt}$.

Rearranging for $M$, we get $M = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{dI/dt}$. The unit of electromotive force $\varepsilon$ is Volt (V), and the unit of $dI/dt$ is Ampere/second (A/s).

Therefore, the unit of $M$ is $\dfrac{\text{Volt}}{\text{Ampere/second}} = \dfrac{\text{Volt} \cdot \text{second}}{\text{Ampere}}$.

Answer: volt. second / ampere

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Around the central part of an air cored solenoid of length $20 \mathrm{~cm}$ and area of cross section $1.4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^2$ and 3000 turns, another coil of 250 turns is closely wound. A current $2 \mathrm{~A}$ in the solenoid is reversed in $0.2 \mathrm{~s}$, then the induced emf produced is
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ inside a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_{0} n I$, where $n = \dfrac{N}{l}$ is the number of turns per unit length.

Given: $N_{1} = 3000$, $l = 0.2 \text{ m}$, $I_{initial} = 2 \text{ A}$, $I_{final} = -2 \text{ A}$, $A = 1.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^2$, $N_{2} = 250$, $\Delta t = 0.2 \text{ s}$.

The magnetic flux $\phi$ through the secondary coil is $\phi = B A = \mu_{0} \left( \dfrac{N_{1}}{l} \right) I A$.

The change in magnetic flux $\Delta \phi$ is $\Delta \phi = \phi_{final} - \phi_{initial} = \mu_{0} \left( \dfrac{N_{1}}{l} \right) A (I_{final} - I_{initial})$.

Substituting the values:
$\Delta \phi = (4 \pi \times 10^{-7}) \times \left( \dfrac{3000}{0.2} \right) \times (1.4 \times 10^{-3}) \times (-2 - 2)$
$\Delta \phi = (4 \pi \times 10^{-7}) \times (15000) \times (1.4 \times 10^{-3}) \times (-4)$
$\Delta \phi = -1.055 \times 10^{-4} \text{ Wb}$ (approx).

The induced emf $\varepsilon$ in the secondary coil is given by Faraday's law: $\varepsilon = -N_{2} \dfrac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t}$.

$\varepsilon = -250 \times \dfrac{-1.055 \times 10^{-4}}{0.2} = 1250 \times 1.055 \times 10^{-4} = 0.131875 \text{ V}$.

Rounding to the nearest value, $\varepsilon \approx 1.32 \times 10^{-1} \text{ V}$.

Answer: $1.32 \times 10^{-1} \mathrm{~V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metallic rod of $2 \mathrm{~m}$ length is rotated with a frequency $100 \mathrm{~Hz}$ about an axis passing through the centre of the circular ring of radius $2 \mathrm{~m}$. A constant magnetic field $2 \mathrm{~T}$ is applied parallel to the axis and perpendicular to the length of the rod. The emf developed across the ends of the rod is :
questions.solution:
The induced emf $e$ across a rod of length $l$ rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$ perpendicular to the plane of rotation is given by the formula $e = \dfrac{1}{2} B \omega l^2$.

Given parameters are:
Length of the rod $l = 2 \text{ m}$
Frequency $f = 100 \text{ Hz}$
Magnetic field $B = 2 \text{ T}$

The angular velocity $\omega$ is calculated as $\omega = 2 \pi f = 2 \pi \times 100 = 200 \pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:
$e = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (200 \pi) \times (2)^2$

$e = 1 \times 200 \pi \times 4$

$e = 800 \pi \text{ V}$.

Answer: 800 $\pi$ volt

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two metal spheres, one of radius $\dfrac{R}{2}$ and the other of radius $2 \mathrm{R}$ respectively have the same surface charge density They are brought in contact and separated. The ratio of their new surface charge densities is
questions.solution:
Let the surface charge density be $\sigma$. The radii of the two spheres are $r_1 = \dfrac{R}{2}$ and $r_2 = 2R$.

The initial charges on the spheres are $q_1 = \sigma \times 4\pi r_1^2 = \sigma \times 4\pi \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 = \sigma \pi R^2$ and $q_2 = \sigma \times 4\pi r_2^2 = \sigma \times 4\pi (2R)^2 = 16\sigma \pi R^2$.

When the spheres are brought into contact, the total charge $Q = q_1 + q_2 = 17\sigma \pi R^2$ is redistributed such that they reach the same potential $V$.

The new charges $q_1'$ and $q_2'$ satisfy $\dfrac{q_1'}{r_1} = \dfrac{q_2'}{r_2}$, which implies $\dfrac{q_1'}{R/2} = \dfrac{q_2'}{2R}$, so $q_2' = 4q_1'$.

Since $q_1' + q_2' = Q$, we have $5q_1' = 17\sigma \pi R^2$, so $q_1' = \dfrac{17}{5}\sigma \pi R^2$ and $q_2' = \dfrac{68}{5}\sigma \pi R^2$.

The new surface charge densities are $\sigma_1' = \dfrac{q_1'}{4\pi r_1^2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{17}{5}\sigma \pi R^2}{4\pi (R/2)^2} = \dfrac{17}{5}\sigma$ and $\sigma_2' = \dfrac{q_2'}{4\pi r_2^2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{68}{5}\sigma \pi R^2}{4\pi (2R)^2} = \dfrac{68}{5 \times 16}\sigma = \dfrac{17}{20}\sigma$.

The ratio $\dfrac{\sigma_1'}{\sigma_2'} = \dfrac{17/5}{17/20} = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4:1$.

Answer: $4: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square shaped aluminium coin weighs $0.75 \mathrm{~g}$ and its diagonal measures $14 \mathrm{~mm}$. It has equal amounts of positive and negative charges. Suppose those equal charges were concentrated in two charges $(+Q$ and $-Q)$ that are separated by a distance equal to the side of the coin, the dipole moment of the dipole is
questions.solution:
The mass of the aluminium coin is $m = 0.75 \text{ g}$. The molar mass of aluminium is $M = 27 \text{ g/mol}$. The number of moles of aluminium is $n = \dfrac{m}{M} = \dfrac{0.75}{27} = \dfrac{1}{36} \text{ mol}$.

The number of atoms in the coin is $N = n \times N_A = \dfrac{1}{36} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 1.67 \times 10^{22}$ atoms. Each aluminium atom has an atomic number $Z = 13$. Thus, the total number of protons (or electrons) in the coin is $N_{total} = N \times Z = 1.67 \times 10^{22} \times 13 \approx 2.17 \times 10^{23}$.

The total charge $Q$ is $N_{total} \times e$, where $e = 1.6 imes 10^{-19} \text{ C}$. So, $Q = 2.17 \times 10^{23} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \approx 3.47 \times 10^4 \text{ C}$.

The diagonal of the square coin is $d = 14 \text{ mm} = 1.4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$. The side length $a$ of the square is given by $a = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1.4 \times 10^{-2}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.99 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

The dipole moment $p$ is given by $p = Q \times a = 3.47 \times 10^4 \times 0.99 \times 10^{-2} \approx 343.5 \text{ Cm}$..

Answer: $343.5 \mathrm{~Cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Five charges, '$q$' each are placed at the comers of a regular pentagon of side '$a$' as shown in figure. First, charge from '$A$' is removed with other charges intact, then charge at '$A$' is replaced with an equal opposite charge. The ratio of magnitudes of electric fields at $\mathrm{O}$, without charge at $A$ and that with equal and opposite charge at $A$ is
questions.solution:
Let the electric field due to a charge $q$ at a corner of the regular pentagon at the center $O$ be $\vec{E}$. The distance from each corner to the center $O$ is $r$.

By symmetry, the sum of the electric fields due to all five charges $q$ at the corners $A, B, C, D, E$ is zero, i.e., $\vec{E}_A + \vec{E}_B + \vec{E}_C + \vec{E}_D + \vec{E}_E = 0$.

When the charge at $A$ is removed, the net electric field at $O$ is $\vec{E}_{net, 1} = \vec{E}_B + \vec{E}_C + \vec{E}_D + \vec{E}_E$. From the symmetry condition, $\vec{E}_{net, 1} = -\vec{E}_A$. The magnitude is $|\vec{E}_{net, 1}| = E$, where $E = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}$.

When the charge at $A$ is replaced by $-q$, the electric field at $O$ due to this new charge is $-\vec{E}_A$. The net electric field at $O$ is $\vec{E}_{net, 2} = \vec{E}_B + \vec{E}_C + \vec{E}_D + \vec{E}_E + \vec{E}_{-A} = -\vec{E}_A - \vec{E}_A = -2\vec{E}_A$. The magnitude is $|\vec{E}_{net, 2}| = 2E$.

The ratio of the magnitudes of the electric fields is $\dfrac{|\vec{E}_{net, 1}|}{|\vec{E}_{net, 2}|} = \dfrac{E}{2E} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: 1 : 2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If potential (in volt) in a region is expressed as $\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}, \mathrm{z})=6 \mathrm{xy}-\mathrm{y}+2 \mathrm{yz}$, the electric field (in $N C^{-1}$) at point $(1,0,1)$ is
questions.solution:
The electric field $\vec{E}$ is related to the potential $V$ by the relation $\vec{E} = -\nabla V = -\left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} \hat{i} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} \hat{j} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} \hat{k} \right)$.

Given $V(x, y, z) = 6xy - y + 2yz$.

Calculating the partial derivatives:
$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(6xy - y + 2yz) = 6y$
$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(6xy - y + 2yz) = 6x - 1 + 2z$
$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}(6xy - y + 2yz) = 2y$

At the point $(1, 0, 1)$:
$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} = 6(0) = 0$
$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} = 6(1) - 1 + 2(1) = 6 - 1 + 2 = 7$
$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} = 2(0) = 0$

Substituting these values into the expression for $\vec{E}$:
$\vec{E} = -(0 \hat{i} + 7 \hat{j} + 0 \hat{k}) = -7 \hat{j}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{-7 j}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charges '$-q$' each are fixed, separated by distance '$2 d$'. A third charge '$q$' of mass '$m$' placed at the mid-point is displaced slightly by '$x$' $(x\lt \lt d)$ perpendicular to the line joining the two fixed charges as shown in Fig. The time period of oscillation of '$q$' will be
questions.solution:
Let the two fixed charges $-q$ be located at $(-d, 0)$ and $(d, 0)$. The charge $q$ is at $(0, x)$. The distance $r$ between the charge $q$ and each of the fixed charges is $r = \sqrt{d^2 + x^2}$.

The force exerted by each fixed charge on $q$ is $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2}$. The vertical component of the force from each charge is $F_y = F \cos \theta$, where $\cos \theta = \dfrac{x}{r}$.

The net restoring force on $q$ is $F_{net} = -2 F_y = -2 \left( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2} \right) \left( \dfrac{x}{r} \right) = -\dfrac{q^2 x}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}$.

Since $x \ll d$, $r = \sqrt{d^2 + x^2} \approx d$. Thus, $F_{net} \approx -\dfrac{q^2 x}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3}$.

The equation of motion is $m \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -\left( \dfrac{q^2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3} \right) x$. This represents simple harmonic motion with angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{q^2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 m d^3}}$.

The time period $T$ is given by $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 m d^3}{q^2}} = \sqrt{4\pi^2 \dfrac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 m d^3}{q^2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8\pi^3 \varepsilon_0 m d^3}{q^2}}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{T}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8 \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{~m} \pi^3 \mathrm{~d}^3}{\mathrm{q}^2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $\mathrm{A}$ is the areal velocity of a planet of mass $\mathrm{M}$, then its angular momentum is
questions.solution:
The areal velocity of a planet is defined as the rate at which the area is swept by the radius vector, given by $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$.

The angular momentum $L$ of a planet of mass $M$ moving in an orbit is given by $L = mvr = mr^2 \omega$, where $\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$.

Substituting $\omega$ into the expression for angular momentum, we get $L = M r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$.

Comparing this with the expression for areal velocity $A = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}$, we see that $r^2 \dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = 2A$.

Therefore, $L = M(2A) = 2MA$.

Answer: $2 \mathrm{MA}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the earth has a mass nine times and radius four times that of planet X, the ratio of the maximum speed required by a rocket to pull out of the gravitational force of planet $\mathrm{X}$ to that of the earth is
questions.solution:
The escape velocity $v_{e}$ of a planet with mass $M$ and radius $R$ is given by the formula $v_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

Let $M_{E}$ and $R_{E}$ be the mass and radius of the Earth, and $M_{X}$ and $R_{X}$ be the mass and radius of planet X. Given $M_{E} = 9M_{X}$ and $R_{E} = 4R_{X}$.

The escape velocity for Earth is $v_{E} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G(9M_{X})}{4R_{X}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4}} \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_{X}}{R_{X}}} = \dfrac{3}{2} v_{X}$, where $v_{X}$ is the escape velocity for planet X.

The ratio of the escape velocity of planet X to that of the Earth is $\dfrac{v_{X}}{v_{E}} = \dfrac{v_{X}}{\dfrac{3}{2} v_{X}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cubical box of side $1 \mathrm{~m}$ contains Boron gas at a pressure of $100 \mathrm{~Nm}^{-2}$. During an observation time of 1 second, an atom travelling with the rms speed parallel to one of the edges of the cube, was found to make 500 hits with a particular wall, without any collision with other atoms. The total mass of gas in the box in gram is
questions.solution:
The side length of the cubical box is $L = 1 \text{ m}$. The volume of the box is $V = L^3 = 1 \text{ m}^3$.

An atom travels with rms speed $v_{rms}$ parallel to an edge. In 1 second, it makes 500 hits on a wall. Since it travels back and forth between two opposite walls, the distance covered in one round trip is $2L = 2 \text{ m}$. The number of hits in 1 second is $N = 500$. The time taken for one round trip is $t = \dfrac{2L}{v_{rms}}$. The number of hits per second is $\dfrac{1}{t} = \dfrac{v_{rms}}{2L}$.

Given $\dfrac{v_{rms}}{2L} = 500$, we have $v_{rms} = 500 \times 2 \times 1 = 1000 \text{ m/s}$.

The pressure of an ideal gas is given by $P = \dfrac{1}{3} \rho v_{rms}^2$, where $\rho = \dfrac{M}{V}$ is the density and $M$ is the total mass of the gas.

Substituting the given values: $100 = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{M}{1} \times (1000)^2$.

$100 = \dfrac{M \times 10^6}{3} \Rightarrow M = \dfrac{300}{10^6} = 3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg}$.

Converting the mass to grams: $M = 3 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^3 \text{ g} = 0.3 \text{ g}$.

Answer: 0.3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An electric bulb of volume $300 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ was sealed off during manufacture at a pressure of $1 \mathrm{~mm}$ of mercury at $27{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The number of air molecules contained in the bulb is,
$(\mathrm{R}=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ , $N_A=6.02 \times 10^{23}$, and $1 \text{ mm of Hg} = 133.3 \text{ N/m}^2$)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone of mass $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ is hung from the ceiling of the room using two strings. If the strings make an angle $60^{\circ}$ and $30^{\circ}$ respectively with the horizontal surface of the roof then the tension on the longer string is : $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$
questions.solution:
The string making $30°$ with the horizontal is longer. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be tensions in strings at $60°$ and $30°$ respectively. Weight $W = mg = 20$ N.

Horizontal equilibrium:
$T_1\cos60° = T_2\cos30°$
$T_1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = T_2 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow T_1 = \sqrt{3}T_2$

Vertical equilibrium:
$T_1\sin60° + T_2\sin30° = 20$

Substituting $T_1 = \sqrt{3}T_2$:
$\sqrt{3}T_2 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + T_2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 20$

$T_2\left(\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 20 \Rightarrow 2T_2 = 20 \Rightarrow T_2 = 10$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two circular coils of radius '$a$' and '$2 a$' are placed coaxially at a distance ' $x$ and '$2 x$' respectively from the origin along the $\mathrm{X}$-axis. If their planes are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the $\mathrm{X}$ - axis and both carry the same current in the same direction, then the ratio of the magnetic field induction at the origin due to the smaller coil to that of the bigger one is:
questions.solution:
The magnetic field $B$ at a distance $d$ along the axis of a circular coil of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is given by the formula $B = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I R^{2}}{2(R^{2} + d^{2})^{3/2}}$.

For the smaller coil, the radius is $R_{1} = a$ and the distance from the origin is $d_{1} = x$. The magnetic field at the origin is $B_{1} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{2(a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}$.

For the bigger coil, the radius is $R_{2} = 2a$ and the distance from the origin is $d_{2} = 2x$. The magnetic field at the origin is $B_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (2a)^{2}}{2((2a)^{2} + (2x)^{2})^{3/2}}$.

Simplifying $B_{2}$: $B_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (4a^{2})}{2(4a^{2} + 4x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (4a^{2})}{2 \times 4^{3/2} (a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I (4a^{2})}{2 \times 8 (a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{4 (a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}$.

The ratio of the magnetic field of the smaller coil to the bigger coil is $\dfrac{B_{1}}{B_{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{2(a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}}{\dfrac{\mu_{0} I a^{2}}{4(a^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2:1$.

Answer: 2 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Current flows through uniform, square frames and their connecting wires as shown in the figure. In which case is the net magnetic field at the centre of the frame not zero?
questions.solution:
The square frame itself always produces zero net field at the centre (symmetric current paths cancel).

Cases A and B: External wires are directed radially (along diagonals) toward/away from the centre \Rightarrow their line of action passes through the centre, so they produce zero field there.

Case D: Incoming and outgoing external wires are on opposite sides and symmetric \Rightarrow their fields cancel at the centre.

Case C: Both external wires are collinear with the top edge and carry current in the same direction (left to right). By the right-hand rule, both produce fields pointing into the page at the centre — they add up instead of cancelling.

Net magnetic field at the centre is non-zero only in Case C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil of radius $0.1 \mathrm{~m}$ is placed in the $\mathrm{X}-\mathrm{Y}$ plane and a current $2 \mathrm{~A}$ is passed through the coil in the clockwise direction when looking from above. Find the magnetic dipole moment of the current loop
questions.solution:
The magnetic dipole moment $\vec{m}$ of a current loop is given by the formula $\vec{m} = I \vec{A}$, where $I$ is the current and $\vec{A}$ is the area vector.

The radius of the coil is $r = 0.1 \text{ m}$. The area of the circular coil is $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.1)^2 = 0.01 \pi \text{ m}^2$.

The current $I = 2 \text{ A}$. The magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment is $m = I A = 2 \times 0.01 \pi = 0.02 \pi \text{ Am}^2$.

The coil is placed in the X-Y plane. According to the right-hand rule, for a clockwise current when viewed from above (looking down the positive Z-axis), the direction of the area vector $\vec{A}$ is along the negative Z-axis. Therefore, the magnetic dipole moment $\vec{m}$ is directed in the negative Z-direction.

Answer: $0.02 \pi \mathrm{Am}^2 \text { in the }-\mathrm{ve} \mathrm{~Z}-\text { direction }$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two similar coils $A$ and $B$ of radius '$r$' and number of turns '$N$' each are placed concentrically with their planes perpendicular to each other. If I and $2 \mathrm{I}$ are the respective currents passing through the coils then the net magnetic induction at the centre of the coils will be:
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular coil of radius $r$ with $N$ turns carrying current $I$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}$.

For coil $A$ with current $I$, the magnetic field is $B_A = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}$.

For coil $B$ with current $2I$, the magnetic field is $B_B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N(2I)}{2r} = \dfrac{2\mu_0 NI}{2r} = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{r}$.

Since the planes of the coils are perpendicular to each other, the magnetic field vectors $\vec{B}_A$ and $\vec{B}_B$ are perpendicular to each other.

The net magnetic induction $B_{net}$ is given by the vector sum $B_{net} = \sqrt{B_A^2 + B_B^2}$.

$B_{net} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{2\mu_0 NI}{2r}\right)^2}$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r} \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2}$

$B_{net} = \sqrt{5} \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}\right)$

Answer: $\sqrt{5}\left(\mu_0 \dfrac{\mathrm{NI}}{2 \mathrm{r}}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Steel is preferred to soft iron for making permanent magnets because,
options: Permeability of steel is slightly greater than soft iron
Steel has more coercivity than soft iron
Susceptibility of steel is less than one
questions.solution:
Permanent magnets are materials that retain their magnetic properties even after the external magnetizing field is removed. This property is known as retentivity.

For a material to be a good permanent magnet, it must have high retentivity and high coercivity. High coercivity ensures that the magnetic state is not easily destroyed by external magnetic fields, temperature fluctuations, or mechanical vibrations.

Soft iron has high permeability and low coercivity, making it ideal for electromagnets where the magnetic field needs to be easily switched on and off. In contrast, steel has lower permeability but significantly higher coercivity compared to soft iron.

Therefore, steel is preferred for making permanent magnets because it retains its magnetism much better due to its higher coercivity.

Answer: Steel has more coercivity than soft iron

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: 64 rain drops of the same radius are falling through air with a steady velocity of $0.5 \mathrm{~cm} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. If the drops coalesce, the terminal velocity would be
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of each small drop and $v$ be its terminal velocity. The terminal velocity of a spherical drop is given by Stokes Law as $v = \dfrac{2}{9} \dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the drop, $\sigma$ is the density of air, and $\eta$ is the coefficient of viscosity. This implies $v \propto r^2$.

When $n = 64$ drops coalesce into a single large drop of radius $R$, the volume remains constant. Thus, $\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = n \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$, which gives $R^3 = n r^3$, or $R = n^{1/3} r$.

Substituting $n = 64$, we get $R = (64)^{1/3} r = 4r$.

Let $V$ be the terminal velocity of the large drop. Since $V \propto R^2$ and $v \propto r^2$, we have $\dfrac{V}{v} = \left( \dfrac{R}{r} \right)^2 = (4)^2 = 16$.

Given $v = 0.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, the terminal velocity of the large drop is $V = 16 \times 0.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 8 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Converting to meters per second, $V = 8 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 0.08 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $0.08 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the ratio of lengths, radii and Young's Moduli of steel and brass wires in the figure are $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}$ and $\mathrm{c}$ respectively, then the corresponding ratio of increase in their lengths would be
questions.solution:
Let $L_s, r_s, Y_s$ be the length, radius, and Young's modulus of the steel wire, and $L_b, r_b, Y_b$ be those of the brass wire. Given ratios are $\dfrac{L_s}{L_b} = a$, $\dfrac{r_s}{r_b} = b$, and $\dfrac{Y_s}{Y_b} = c$.

The tension in the steel wire is $T_s = 2Mg$ (supporting the $2M$ mass). The tension in the brass wire is $T_b = (M + 2M)g = 3Mg$ (supporting both masses).

The elongation $\Delta L$ is given by $\Delta L = \dfrac{TL}{AY} = \dfrac{TL}{\pi r^2 Y}$.

The ratio of increase in lengths is $\dfrac{\Delta L_s}{\Delta L_b} = \dfrac{T_s L_s}{\pi r_s^2 Y_s} \times \dfrac{\pi r_b^2 Y_b}{T_b L_b} = \left( \dfrac{T_s}{T_b} \right) \left( \dfrac{L_s}{L_b} \right) \left( \dfrac{r_b}{r_s} \right)^2 \left( \dfrac{Y_b}{Y_s} \right)$.

Substituting the given values: $\dfrac{T_s}{T_b} = \dfrac{2Mg}{3Mg} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, $\dfrac{L_s}{L_b} = a$, $\dfrac{r_b}{r_s} = \dfrac{1}{b}$, and $\dfrac{Y_b}{Y_s} = \dfrac{1}{c}$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{\Delta L_s}{\Delta L_b} = \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right) (a) \left( \dfrac{1}{b^2} \right) \left( \dfrac{1}{c} \right) = \dfrac{2a}{3b^2c}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 a}{3 b^2 c}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When two objects are moving along a straight line in the same direction, the distance between them increases by $6 \mathrm{~m}$ in one second. If the objects move with their constant speed towards each other the distance decreases by $8 \mathrm{~m}$ in one second, then the speed of the objects are :
questions.solution:
Let the speeds of the two objects be $v_1$ and $v_2$ in $\text{ms}^{-1}$, where $v_1 \gt v_2$.

When moving in the same direction, the relative speed is $v_1 - v_2$. The distance between them increases by $6 \text{ m}$ in $1 \text{ s}$, so $v_1 - v_2 = \dfrac{6 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ s}} = 6 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

When moving towards each other, the relative speed is $v_1 + v_2$. The distance between them decreases by $8 \text{ m}$ in $1 \text{ s}$, so $v_1 + v_2 = \dfrac{8 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ s}} = 8 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Adding the two equations: $(v_1 - v_2) + (v_1 + v_2) = 6 + 8 \Rightarrow 2v_1 = 14 \Rightarrow v_1 = 7 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Subtracting the first equation from the second: $(v_1 + v_2) - (v_1 - v_2) = 8 - 6 \Rightarrow 2v_2 = 2 \Rightarrow v_2 = 1 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The speeds of the objects are $7 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ and $1 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $7 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ and $1 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is moving along a circular path of radius '$r$' with a frequency of revolution numerically equal to the radius of the circular path. What is the acceleration of the body if radius of the path is $\left(\dfrac{5}{\pi}\right) m$ ?
questions.solution:
The acceleration of a body moving in a circular path is the centripetal acceleration, given by $a = \omega^2 r$.

The angular velocity $\omega$ is related to the frequency $f$ by the formula $\omega = 2 \pi f$.

Given that the frequency $f$ is numerically equal to the radius $r$, we have $f = r$.

Substituting $f = r$ into the expression for $\omega$, we get $\omega = 2 \pi r$.

The acceleration $a$ becomes $a = (2 \pi r)^2 r = 4 \pi^2 r^3$.

Given the radius $r = \dfrac{5}{\pi}$ m, we substitute this value into the expression for $a$:

$a = 4 \pi^2 \left( \dfrac{5}{\pi} \right)^3$

$a = 4 \pi^2 \left( \dfrac{125}{\pi^3} \right)$

$a = \dfrac{4 \times 125}{\pi} = \dfrac{500}{\pi} \text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{500}{\pi}\right) \mathrm{ms}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal ball of $20 \mathrm{~g}$ is projected at an angle $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal with an initial velocity $10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. If the mass and angle of projection are doubled keeping the initial velocity the same, the ratio of the maximum height attained in the former to the latter case is :
questions.solution:
The maximum height $H$ attained by a projectile is given by the formula $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$, where $u$ is the initial velocity, $\theta$ is the angle of projection, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

In the first case, $u_1 = 10 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ and $\theta_1 = 30^{\circ}$. The maximum height is $H_1 = \dfrac{u_1^2 \sin^2(30^{\circ})}{2g} = \dfrac{10^2 \times (1/2)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{100 \times 1/4}{2g} = \dfrac{25}{2g}$.

In the second case, the mass is doubled (which does not affect the height), the velocity remains $u_2 = 10 \text{ ms}^{-1}$, and the angle is doubled, so $\theta_2 = 2 \times 30^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}$. The maximum height is $H_2 = \dfrac{u_2^2 \sin^2(60^{\circ})}{2g} = \dfrac{10^2 \times (\sqrt{3}/2)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{100 \times 3/4}{2g} = \dfrac{75}{2g}$.

The ratio of the maximum height in the former case to the latter case is $\dfrac{H_1}{H_2} = \dfrac{25/2g}{75/2g} = \dfrac{25}{75} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

Answer: 1 : 3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The closest approach of an alpha particle when it make a head on collision with a gold nucleus is $10 \times 10^{-14} \mathrm{~m}$, then the kinetic energy of the alpha particle is :
questions.solution:
The distance of closest approach $r_0$ for an alpha particle of kinetic energy $K$ colliding head-on with a nucleus of atomic number $Z$ is given by the conservation of energy:

$K = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{(Ze)(2e)}{r_0}$

For a gold nucleus, the atomic number $Z = 79$. The value of the Coulomb constant is $\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-2}$. The charge of an electron is $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

Substituting the given values $r_0 = 10 \times 10^{-14} \text{ m} = 10^{-13} \text{ m}$:

$K = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^9) \times (79 \times 2) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{10^{-13}}$

$K = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 158 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{10^{-13}}$

$K = 9 \times 158 \times 2.56 \times 10^{9 - 38 + 13}$

$K = 3640.32 \times 10^{-16} \text{ J}$

$K = 3.64032 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$

Rounding to the nearest value, we get $K = 3.64 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$.

Answer: $3.64 \times 10^{-13} \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of the radii of the nucleus of two element $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ having the mass numbers 232 and 29 is:
questions.solution:
The radius of a nucleus is given by the formula $R = R_{0} A^{1/3}$, where $R_{0}$ is a constant and $A$ is the mass number of the nucleus.

For the two elements X and Y, the ratio of their radii is given by $\dfrac{R_{X}}{R_{Y}} = \dfrac{R_{0} A_{X}^{1/3}}{R_{0} A_{Y}^{1/3}} = \left( \dfrac{A_{X}}{A_{Y}} \right)^{1/3}$.

Given $A_{X} = 232$ and $A_{Y} = 29$, we substitute these values into the ratio:

$\dfrac{R_{X}}{R_{Y}} = \left( \dfrac{232}{29} \right)^{1/3}$.

Since $232 = 29 \times 8$, we have $\dfrac{232}{29} = 8$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{R_{X}}{R_{Y}} = (8)^{1/3} = 2$.

The ratio is $2 : 1$.

Answer: 2 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Find the binding energy of the tritium nucleus:
[Given: mass of $1 \mathrm{H}^3=3.01605 \mathrm{~u} ; \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}}=1.00782 \mathrm{~u} ; \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{n}}=1.00866 \mathrm{~u}$.]
questions.solution:
The tritium nucleus $^{3}_{1}H$ consists of 1 proton and 2 neutrons.

Mass of constituents = $m_p + 2m_n = 1.00782 + 2 \times 1.00866 = 1.00782 + 2.01732 = 3.02514 \text{ u}$.

Mass defect $\Delta m = (m_p + 2m_n) - m_{nucleus} = 3.02514 - 3.01605 = 0.00909 \text{ u}$.

Binding energy = $\Delta m \times 931.5 \text{ MeV/u} = 0.00909 \times 931.5 \approx 8.467 \text{ MeV}$.

Rounding to the nearest given option, the binding energy is approximately 8.5 MeV.

Answer: 8.5 MeV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle executes a simple harmonic motion of amplitude $\mathrm{A}$. The distance from the mean position at which its kinetic energy is equal to its potential energy is
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy $K$ and potential energy $U$ of a particle executing simple harmonic motion with amplitude $A$ at a distance $x$ from the mean position are given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2} k(A^2 - x^2)$ and $U = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2$, where $k$ is the force constant.

Given that the kinetic energy is equal to the potential energy, we set $K = U$:

$\dfrac{1}{2} k(A^2 - x^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^2$

Simplifying the equation:

$A^2 - x^2 = x^2$

$A^2 = 2x^2$

$x^2 = \dfrac{A^2}{2}$

$x = \dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$

Using the value $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$, we calculate:

$x = \dfrac{A}{1.414} \approx 0.707 A$

Rounding to two decimal places, we get $x = 0.71 A$.

Answer: 0.71 A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a $30^{\circ}$ prism when a ray of light is incident at an angle $60^{\circ}$ on one of its faces, the emergent ray passes normal to the other surface. Then the refractive index of the prism is:
questions.solution:
Given the prism angle $A = 30^{\circ}$. The angle of incidence $i = 60^{\circ}$. The emergent ray passes normal to the other surface, which means the angle of emergence $e = 0^{\circ}$.

From the geometry of the prism, the angle of refraction at the first surface $r_1$ and the angle of incidence at the second surface $r_2$ satisfy $r_1 + r_2 = A$.

Since the emergent ray is normal to the second surface, $r_2 = 0^{\circ}$. Therefore, $r_1 + 0^{\circ} = 30^{\circ}$, which gives $r_1 = 30^{\circ}$.

Applying Snell's law at the first surface, $\mu = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r_1}$.

Substituting the values, $\mu = \dfrac{\sin 60^{\circ}}{\sin 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} = \sqrt{3}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ray of light travelling through a medium of refractive index $\dfrac{5}{4}$ is incident on a glass of refractive index $\dfrac{3}{2}$. Find the angle of refraction in the glass, if the angle of incidence at the given medium - glass interface is $30^{\circ}$.
questions.solution:
Given the refractive index of the first medium $n_1 = \dfrac{5}{4}$ and the refractive index of the second medium (glass) $n_2 = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

The angle of incidence $i = 30^{\circ}$.

Using Snell's Law, $n_1 \sin(i) = n_2 \sin(r)$, where $r$ is the angle of refraction.

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{5}{4} \sin(30^{\circ}) = \dfrac{3}{2} \sin(r)$

Since $\sin(30^{\circ}) = \dfrac{1}{2}$, we have:

$\dfrac{5}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} \sin(r)$

$\dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{3}{2} \sin(r)$

$\sin(r) = \dfrac{5}{8} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{10}{24} = \dfrac{5}{12}$

Therefore, $r = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right)$.

Answer: $\sin ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the normal adjustment of an astronomical telescope, the objective and eyepiece are $32 \mathrm{~cm}$ apart. If the magnifying power of the telescope is 7, find the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece.
questions.solution:
justment is given by $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$.

Given $M = 7$, we have $\dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = 7$, which implies $f_o = 7f_e$.

Substituting $f_o = 7f_e$ into the first equation: $7f_e + f_e = 32$.

$8f_e = 32 \Rightarrow f_e = 4 \text{ cm}$.

Using $f_o = 7f_e$, we get $f_o = 7 \times 4 = 28 \text{ cm}$.

Therefore, $f_o = 28 \text{ cm}$ and $f_e = 4 \text{ cm}$.

Answer: $f_o=28 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $f_e=4 \mathrm{~cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a particular wave length of light is used the focal length of a convex mirror is found to be $10 \mathrm{~cm}$. If the wave length of the incident light is doubled keeping the area of the mirror constant, the focal length of the mirror will be:
questions.solution:
The focal length $f$ of a spherical mirror is given by the relation $f = \dfrac{R}{2}$, where $R$ is the radius of curvature of the mirror.

The radius of curvature $R$ depends only on the geometry and the physical dimensions of the mirror surface. It is determined by the radius of the sphere from which the mirror is cut.

The focal length of a mirror is independent of the wavelength of the incident light. Changing the wavelength of the light does not alter the physical shape or the radius of curvature of the mirror.

Since the area of the mirror is kept constant, the radius of curvature $R$ remains unchanged. Therefore, the focal length remains $10 \text{ cm}$.

Answer: 10 cm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $5 \mathrm{~kg}$ at rest is rotated for $25 \mathrm{~s}$ with a constant moment of force $10 \mathrm{~Nm}$. Find the work done if the moment of inertia of the body is $5 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^2$.
questions.solution:
Given the moment of force (torque) $\tau = 10 \text{ Nm}$, moment of inertia $I = 5 \text{ kg m}^2$, and time $t = 25 \text{ s}$.

The angular acceleration $\alpha$ is given by $\tau = I \alpha$.

$\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2 \text{ rad/s}^2$.

Since the body starts from rest, the initial angular velocity $\omega_0 = 0$. The angular velocity after time $t$ is $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t = 0 + 2 \times 25 = 50 \text{ rad/s}$.

The work done is equal to the change in rotational kinetic energy $W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega_0^2$.

$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times (50)^2 - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 2500 = 5 \times 1250 = 6250 \text{ J}$.

Answer: 6250 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a given semiconductor, the ratio of the number density of electron to number density of hole is $2: 1$. If $\dfrac{1}{7}$th of the total current is due to the hole and the remaining is due to the electrons, the ratio of the drift velocity of holes to the drift velocity of electrons is :
questions.solution:
Let $n_e$ and $n_h$ be the number densities of electrons and holes respectively. Given $\dfrac{n_e}{n_h} = \dfrac{2}{1}$, so $n_e = 2n_h$.

The total current $I$ is the sum of electron current $I_e$ and hole current $I_h$. Given $I_h = \dfrac{1}{7}I$, it follows that $I_e = I - I_h = \dfrac{6}{7}I$.

The current is given by $I = nqvA$, where $n$ is number density, $q$ is charge magnitude, $v$ is drift velocity, and $A$ is cross-sectional area. Thus, $I_e = n_e e v_e A$ and $I_h = n_h e v_h A$.

Taking the ratio of $I_h$ to $I_e$:

$\dfrac{I_h}{I_e} = \dfrac{n_h e v_h A}{n_e e v_e A} = \dfrac{n_h v_h}{n_e v_e}$

Substituting the known values:

$\dfrac{1/7}{6/7} = \dfrac{n_h v_h}{2n_h v_e}$

$\dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{v_h}{2v_e}$

$\dfrac{v_h}{v_e} = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Though $\mathrm{Sn}$ and $\mathrm{Si}$ are $4^{\text {th }}$ group elements, $\mathrm{Sn}$ is a metal while $\mathrm{Si}$ is a semiconductor because
options: The energy gap of $\mathrm{Sn}$ is zero volt while that of $\mathrm{Si}$ is $0.07 \mathrm{~V}$
The energy gap of $\mathrm{Sn}$ is $1.1 \mathrm{~eV}$ volt while that of $\mathrm{Si}$ is $0.07 \mathrm{~V}$
questions.solution:
The electrical nature of a material depends on the energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band.

In Sn (white tin), the valence and conduction bands overlap, giving an effective energy gap of zero. Electrons can move freely, making it a metal.

In Si, there is a small but finite energy gap (~1.1 eV), allowing only limited electron excitation at room temperature, making it a semiconductor.

Among the given options, the defining characteristic is that the energy gap of Sn is zero while that of Si is finite (given as 0.07 V in the options). The correct option is (2).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal diode is connected in series with a capacitor. The free ends of the capacitor and the diode are connected across a $220 \mathrm{~V}$ ac source. Now the potential difference across the capacitor is :
questions.solution:
The input voltage is an AC source given by $V(t) = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, where $V_{rms} = 220 \text{ V}$. The peak voltage $V_0$ is given by $V_0 = V_{rms} \sqrt{2} = 220 \sqrt{2} \approx 311 \text{ V}$.

The circuit consists of an ideal diode in series with a capacitor. During the positive half-cycle of the AC source, the diode is forward-biased and acts as a short circuit. The capacitor charges up to the peak value of the input voltage, which is $V_0 = 311 \text{ V}$.

During the negative half-cycle, the diode becomes reverse-biased and acts as an open circuit. Since the diode prevents the discharge of the capacitor, the capacitor retains its charge and remains at the peak potential difference of $311 \text{ V}$.

Therefore, the potential difference across the capacitor is $311 \text{ V}$.

Answer: $311 \mathrm{~V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A one $\mathrm{kg}$ block of ice at $-1.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ falls from a height of $1.5 \mathrm{~km}$ and is found melting. The amount of ice melted due to fall, if $60 \%$ energy is converted into heat is (Specific heat capacity of ice is $0.5 \mathrm{~cal} \mathrm{~g}^{-1} \mathrm{~C}^{-1}$, Latent heat of fusion of ice $=80 \mathrm{~cal~g}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
PE lost $= mgh = 1 \times 9.8 \times 1500 = 14700$ J

Heat generated $= 0.6 \times 14700 = 8820$ J $= \dfrac{8820}{4.2} = 2100$ cal

Heat to warm ice from $-1.5°C$ to $0°C$:
$Q_1 = 1000 \times 0.5 \times 1.5 = 750$ cal

Heat available for melting:
$Q_{melt} = 2100 - 750 = 1350$ cal

Mass melted $= \dfrac{Q_{melt}}{L} = \dfrac{1350}{80} \approx 16.9$ g

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A glass of hot water cools from $90^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $70^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in 3 minutes when the temperature of surroundings is $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. What is the time taken by the glass of hot water to cool from $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ if the surrounding temperature remains the same at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?
questions.solution:
According to Newton's law of cooling, the rate of cooling is given by $\dfrac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_s)$, where $T$ is the temperature of the body, $T_s$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k$ is a constant.

For the first interval, $T_1 = 90^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_2 = 70^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_s = 20^{\circ} \text{C}$, and $t = 3 \text{ minutes}$. Using the average temperature approximation $\dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k \left( \dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_s \right)$, we get $\dfrac{90 - 70}{3} = k \left( \dfrac{90 + 70}{2} - 20 \right)$.

$\dfrac{20}{3} = k(80 - 20) = 60k$, which implies $k = \dfrac{20}{3 \times 60} = \dfrac{1}{9}$.

For the second interval, $T_1 = 60^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_2 = 40^{\circ} \text{C}$, $T_s = 20^{\circ} \text{C}$, and we need to find $t'$. Using the same formula, $\dfrac{60 - 40}{t'} = k \left( \dfrac{60 + 40}{2} - 20 \right)$.

$\dfrac{20}{t'} = \dfrac{1}{9} (50 - 20) = \dfrac{30}{9} = \dfrac{10}{3}$.

Solving for $t'$, $t' = \dfrac{20 \times 3}{10} = 6 \text{ minutes}$.

Answer: 6 minutes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Find the value of '$n$' in the given equation $P=\rho^n v^2$ where '$P$' is the pressure, '$\rho$' density and '$v$' velocity.
questions.solution:
The dimensional formula for pressure $P$ is $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

The dimensional formula for density $\rho$ is $[M L^{-3}]$.

The dimensional formula for velocity $v$ is $[L T^{-1}]$.

Substituting these into the equation $P = \rho^n v^2$, we get:

$[M L^{-1} T^{-2}] = [M L^{-3}]^n [L T^{-1}]^2$

$[M L^{-1} T^{-2}] = [M^n L^{-3n}] [L^2 T^{-2}]$

$[M L^{-1} T^{-2}] = [M^n L^{-3n+2} T^{-2}]$

Comparing the powers of $M$ on both sides, we get $n = 1$.

Checking the powers of $L$: $-1 = -3n + 2 \Rightarrow 3n = 3 \Rightarrow n = 1$.

Checking the powers of $T$: $-2 = -2$, which is consistent.

Answer: $\mathrm{n}=1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the given dimensional formula represents heat capacity
questions.solution:
Heat capacity $C$ is defined as the amount of heat energy $Q$ required to raise the temperature of a substance by an amount $\Delta T$.

The formula is $C = \dfrac{Q}{\Delta T}$.

The dimensional formula for heat energy $Q$ is the same as work or energy, which is $[ML^2T^{-2}]$.

The dimensional formula for temperature change $\Delta T$ is $[K]$.

Substituting these into the formula, we get $C = \dfrac{[ML^2T^{-2}]}{[K]} = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The width of the fringes obtained in the Young's double slit experiment is $2.6 \mathrm{~mm}$ when light of wave length $6000^{\circ} \mathrm{A}$ is used. If the whole apparatus is immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.3 the new fringe width will be :
questions.solution:
The fringe width $\beta$ in Young's double slit experiment is given by the formula $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of light, $D$ is the distance between the slits and the screen, and $d$ is the distance between the slits.

When the apparatus is immersed in a liquid of refractive index $\mu$, the wavelength of light changes to $\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}$.

The new fringe width $\beta'$ is given by $\beta' = \dfrac{\lambda' D}{d} = \dfrac{\lambda D}{\mu d} = \dfrac{\beta}{\mu}$.

Given $\beta = 2.6 \text{ mm}$ and $\mu = 1.3$, we have $\beta' = \dfrac{2.6}{1.3} \text{ mm} = 2 \text{ mm}$.

Answer: 2 mm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the Young's double slit experiment $n^{\text {th }}$ bright for red coincides with $(n+1)^{\text {th }}$ bright for violet. Then the value of '$n$' is: (given: wave length of red light $=6300^{\circ} \mathrm{A}$ and wave length of violet $=4200^{\circ} \mathrm{A}$).
questions.solution:
The condition for the $n^{\text{th}}$ bright fringe of red light to coincide with the $(n+1)^{\text{th}}$ bright fringe of violet light is given by the path difference equality:

$n \lambda_{R} = (n+1) \lambda_{V}$

Given $\lambda_{R} = 6300 \text{ \AA}$ and $\lambda_{V} = 4200 \text{ \AA}$, substituting these values into the equation:

$n \times 6300 = (n+1) \times 4200$

Dividing both sides by 2100:

$n \times 3 = (n+1) \times 2$

$3n = 2n + 2$

$n = 2$

Answer: 2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When light wave passes from a medium of refractive index '$\mu$' to another medium of refractive index '$2 \mu$' the phase change occurs to the light is :
questions.solution:
When light passes (transmits) from one medium into another, the transmitted wave undergoes no phase change, regardless of whether it enters a denser or rarer medium.

A phase change of $180°$ occurs only during reflection at a boundary with a denser medium — not during transmission.

Since the light here is passing (transmitting) from medium $\mu$ into medium $2\mu$, the phase change is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a single slit diffraction experiment, for slit width '$\alpha$' the width of the central maxima is '$\beta$'. If we double the slit width then the corresponding width of the central maxima will be:
questions.solution:
The angular width of the central maximum in a single slit diffraction experiment is given by the formula $\theta = \dfrac{2\lambda}{a}$, where $a$ is the slit width and $\lambda$ is the wavelength of light.

The linear width of the central maximum on a screen at a distance $D$ from the slit is given by $\beta = D \times \theta = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}$.

From this expression, it is evident that the width of the central maximum $\beta$ is inversely proportional to the slit width $a$, i.e., $\beta \propto \dfrac{1}{a}$.

Let the initial slit width be $a_1 = a$ and the initial width of the central maximum be $\beta_1 = \beta$.

When the slit width is doubled, the new slit width $a_2 = 2a$.

The new width of the central maximum $\beta_2$ is given by $\beta_2 = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a_2} = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{2a} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a} \right) = \dfrac{\beta}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\beta}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string of length $25 \mathrm{~cm}$ and mass $10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg}$ is clamped at its ends. The tension in the string is $2.5 \mathrm{~N}$. The identical wave pulses are generated at one end and at regular interval of time, $\Delta \mathrm{t}$. The minimum value of $\Delta \mathrm{t}$, so that a constructive interference takes place between successive pulses is
questions.solution:
The linear mass density $\mu$ of the string is given by $\mu = \dfrac{M}{L} = \dfrac{10^{-3} \text{ kg}}{0.25 \text{ m}} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg/m}$.

The speed of the wave $v$ in the string is $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2.5}{4 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2500}{4}} = \sqrt{625} = 25 \text{ m/s}$.

The time taken for a pulse to travel from one end to the other is $t = \dfrac{L}{v} = \dfrac{0.25 \text{ m}}{25 \text{ m/s}} = 0.01 \text{ s} = 10 \text{ ms}$.

For constructive interference between successive pulses, the pulses must return to the starting point in phase. A pulse travels to the other end (10 ms), reflects (phase change of $\pi$), and returns to the starting end (another 10 ms). The total time for a pulse to return to the start is $2t = 20 \text{ ms}$.

Since the pulse reflects at the fixed end with a phase shift of $\pi$, the next pulse must be sent such that it arrives at the start at the same time as the reflected pulse to interfere constructively. The minimum time interval $\Delta t$ is equal to the time taken for the round trip, which is $20 \text{ ms}$.

Answer: 20 ms

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The power of a gun which fires 120 bullet per minute with a velocity $120 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ is : (given the mass of each bullet is $100 \mathrm{~g}$)
questions.solution:
The number of bullets fired per second is $n = \dfrac{120}{60} = 2$ bullets per second.

The mass of each bullet is $m = 100 \text{ g} = 0.1 \text{ kg}$.

The velocity of each bullet is $v = 120 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The kinetic energy of one bullet is $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.1 \times (120)^2 = 0.05 \times 14400 = 720 \text{ J}$.

The power of the gun is the total kinetic energy delivered per second, which is $P = n \times K = 2 \times 720 = 1440 \text{ W}$.

Converting to kilowatts, $P = \dfrac{1440}{1000} \text{ kW} = 1.44 \text{ kW}$.

Answer: 1.44 kW
